extracted.intended_audience: editors, journal owners, publishers, peer reviewers, and authors involved in medical journal publishing
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and recommendations (ICMJE) for conduct, reporting, editing, and publication in medical journals, covering responsibilities of reviewers, editors, owners, authors, and journals' policies (ethics, corrections, preprints, supplements, advertising, electronic publishing, media interactions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should respond promptly to review requests and submit reviews within the agreed time; comments should be constructive, honest, and polite; reviewers should declare relationships and activities that might bias their evaluation and recuse themselves if a conflict exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should be aware that AI can generate authoritative-sounding but incorrect, incomplete, or biased output. Declare conflicts and recuse if necessary. Timeliness and tone are expected; honesty and constructiveness guide content of reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governance and statement of owner–editor relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: A medical journal should explicitly state its governance and relationship to a journal owner (e.g., a sponsoring society).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity about governance helps manage differing responsibilities of owners and editors and potential conflicts; should be disclosed publicly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Owner responsibilities for editor appointment and contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Owners are responsible for appointing and dismissing editors and should provide editors at appointment with a contract that clearly states their rights and duties, authority, general terms of appointment, and mechanisms for resolving conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor performance may be assessed using mutually agreed-upon measures (readership, manuscript submissions and handling times, journal metrics). Owners should not interfere arbitrarily; contractual clarity protects editorial independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds and process for editor dismissal
rubrics_metrics.description: Owners should only dismiss editors for substantial reasons — e.g., scientific misconduct; disagreement with long-term editorial direction; inadequate performance by agreed metrics; or inappropriate behavior incompatible with a position of trust — and appointments/dismissals should be based on evaluations by a panel of independent experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dismissals should not be made unilaterally by a small number of executives; independent expert panels are recommended, especially given importance of freedom of speech in science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors-in-chief should have full authority over the entire editorial content of their journal and the timing of publication; journal owners should not interfere in evaluation, selection, scheduling, or editing of individual articles or create an environment that strongly influences decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial decisions should be based on validity of the work and its importance to readers, not commercial implications. Editors should be free to express critical but responsible views about medicine without fear of retribution. Editors should also have final say over advertisements, sponsored content (including supplements), use of the journal brand, and overall policy regarding commercial use of content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor access and advocacy for editorial freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: To secure editorial freedom in practice, the editor should have direct access to the highest level of ownership, not a delegated manager; editors and editors’ organizations should support editorial freedom and draw attention to major transgressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct access reduces undue influence; editorial organizations should publicly call out breaches of editorial independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental responsibility of journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors, publishers, journal owners, and other stakeholders should work together to develop immediate strategies to reduce carbon emissions, with a goal toward achieving net zero carbon emissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges medical publishing's contribution to carbon emissions; joint strategies across stakeholders are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality, fact-checking, and legal support
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should defend confidentiality of authors and peer reviewers and take reasonable steps to check facts in journal commentary (including news and social media postings), ensure staff adhere to journalistic best practices, and secure appropriate legal advice and insurance when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices such as contemporaneous note-taking and seeking responses from all parties before publication help defend against libel; owners should ensure legal advice and insurance availability; editors should inform legal advisers and owners promptly if legal problems arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics approval and adherence to Helsinki Declaration
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigators should ensure planning, conduct, and reporting of human research are in accordance with the Helsinki Declaration (revised 2024). Authors should seek approval from an independent local, regional, or national review body and be prepared to provide documentation; if doubt exists authors must explain rationale and demonstrate explicit approval for doubtful aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approval by a review body does not preclude editors forming their own judgment about appropriateness of research conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patient privacy and informed consent for publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Patients have a right to privacy; identifying information (names, initials, hospital numbers, photographs, pedigrees) should not be published unless essential and the patient (or guardian) gives written informed consent after being shown the manuscript and informed about potential online availability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consent should be written and archived (by journal or author, per local laws). Journals should require informed consent in author instructions and indicate when consent has been obtained. Nonessential identifying details should be omitted; masking eye region is inadequate; deidentification must not distort scientific meaning; if anonymity is doubtful obtain consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting of animal experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting experiments on animals, authors should indicate whether institutional and national standards for the care and use of laboratory animals were followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear statement regarding adherence to standards should be included in manuscripts involving animal research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections and version control — minimum standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should publish a correction notice promptly detailing changes and citing the original; post a new article version with details of changes and dates; archive all prior versions (accessible or on request); previous electronic versions should note that more recent versions exist; citations should be to the most recent version.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrections needed for factual errors that should have been recognized at publication. Archiving and clear versioning ensure transparent indexing and citation practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling pervasive errors, retraction, and republication
rubrics_metrics.description: Pervasive errors from coding or miscalculation may require correction if they do not change conclusions; errors serious enough to invalidate results may require retraction. Retraction with republication can be considered for unintentional errors where the underlying science remains valid and a revised paper survives further review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When republishing after retraction, show extent of changes in supplementary material or appendix for transparency. For older publications (e.g., >10 years), practical constraints may make correction less warranted; editors may reasonably decline correction if impact is minimal or authors/data unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and handling of scientific misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific misconduct includes (but is not limited to) data fabrication; data falsification (including deceptive image manipulation); purposeful failure to disclose relationships and activities; and plagiarism. Failure to publish clinical trial results may be considered misconduct by some.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When misconduct is alleged, editors should initiate appropriate procedures (e.g., COPE), consider informing institutions and funders, and may publish an expression of concern pending outcomes. Editors should seek investigation outcomes and publish retractions if misconduct is proven; where misconduct is unproven, letters to the editor may highlight debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format, labeling, and linking of expressions of concern and retractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions of concern and retractions should be prominently labeled, appear on an electronic or numbered print page included in the Table of Contents to ensure indexing, include in their heading the title of the original article, be linked in both directions online, and the retracted article should be clearly labeled as retracted in all forms (abstract, full text, PDF).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text of retraction should explain why the article is being retracted and include a complete citation. Authors of the retraction should ideally be the same as the article's authors; if not, under certain circumstances the editor or other responsible persons may author the retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention and public labeling of retracted articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Retracted articles should remain in the public domain and be clearly labeled as retracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may ask institutions to assure validity of other work by authors of fraudulent papers or may retract other papers; if assurance is not provided, editors may publish announcements expressing concern about the validity of prior work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright clarity and policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should make clear the type of copyright under which work will be published and, if the journal retains copyright, detail the position on transfer of copyright for all content types (audio, video, protocols, data sets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals may require transfer of copyright, a publication license, or rely on Creative Commons or other licenses. Some content (e.g., certain government works) may not be copyrightable; editors may waive copyright on content. Policies should be transparent and clearly stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on duplicate submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should not submit the same manuscript, in the same or different languages, simultaneously to more than one journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duplicate submission can create disputes about publication rights and leads to unnecessary peer-review and editing work by multiple journals; authors who attempt duplicate submission should expect prompt rejection and possible retraction if already published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplicate and prior publication disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Duplicate publication is publication overlapping substantially with one already published without clear, visible reference to the previous publication. Authors submitting manuscripts that overlap substantially with published or submitted work should disclose this in the submission letter and provide copies of related material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all prior dissemination counts as duplicate publication (e.g., preliminary reports, abstracts, posters, assessment reports by regulators). Editors may consider submissions that follow preliminary reports; authors should inform journals about related works and preprints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprint archive selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should choose preprint archives that: clearly identify preprints as not peer-reviewed; require authors to document disclosures of interest; require authors to indicate funding sources; have a clear process for users to notify administrators about concerns (public commenting desirable); maintain metadata for withdrawn preprints and post withdrawal notices with timing and reason; and provide a mechanism for authors to indicate subsequent peer-reviewed publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing archives with these features maximizes benefits and minimizes harms of disseminating non–peer-reviewed findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submitting manuscripts that are posted as preprints
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should inform a journal if the submitted work has been posted on a preprint server and provide a link to the preprint (whether posting occurs prior to submission or during peer review); it is helpful to indicate in the manuscript that a preprint is available and how to access it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors are responsible for amending preprints to point readers to subsequent versions (including the final published article). Authors should not post the published article nor interim peer-review–informed revised versions to the preprint archive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referencing preprints in manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: When preprints are cited, the citation should clearly indicate that the reference is a preprint; when the preprint has been published in a peer-reviewed journal, cite the published article rather than the preprint whenever appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the word 'preprint' in the reference list and consider indicating it in text. Include link and DOI if available. Be cautious about citing preprints never subsequently published; time intervals of concern vary by topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for acceptable secondary publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary (re)publication may be justifiable to disseminate important information provided specific conditions are met: (1) authors have approval from both journals' editors (secondary editor must access primary version); (2) priority of primary publication is respected by a negotiated interval; (3) the secondary paper is intended for a different group of readers (an abbreviated version may suffice); (4) the secondary version faithfully reflects authors, data, and interpretations of the primary version; (5) the secondary version informs readers that it has been published elsewhere and cites the primary reference; (6) the title should indicate that it is a secondary publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translations are not considered 'republications' by NLM when original article was in an indexed journal. When publishing simultaneously in multiple languages, MEDLINE notes multiple languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscripts derived from the same database
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts from separate groups or the same group analyzing the same data set should be considered independently as they may differ in analytic methods or conclusions. Manuscripts should add substantially to each other to warrant separate publication and should cite previous publications from the same data set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If interpretations and conclusions are similar, preference to the manuscript submitted first may be reasonable but is not mandatory. Secondary analyses of clinical trial data should cite the primary publication, clearly state they are secondary analyses, and use the same trial registration number and persistent data set identifier. Transparency about planned multiple publications and registration is key.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision for correspondence and post-publication critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should provide mechanisms (correspondence section or online forum) for readers to submit comments, questions, or criticisms; authors of discussed articles have responsibility to respond to substantial criticisms via the same mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors of correspondence should declare competing interests. Correspondence may be edited for length and style or published unedited (e.g., online commenting). Editors must screen discourteous, inaccurate, or libellous comments. Editors may reject correspondence that is irrelevant, uninteresting, or lacking cogency, while promoting a range of opinions and debate. Journals may set time limits for responding to published material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about fees and revenue streams
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should be transparent about their types of revenue streams. Any fees or charges required for manuscript processing and/or publishing should be clearly stated in an easy-to-find place prior to submission or explained to authors before manuscript preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow best-practice transparency guidelines; make fee policies accessible to potential authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles for supplements, theme issues, and special series
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplements (and externally funded theme issues/special series) should be governed by principles: (1) the journal editor must have full responsibility and take full responsibility for policies, practices, and content of supplements; (2) editor may appoint external editors but retains responsibility; (3) editor must retain authority to send supplement manuscripts for external peer review and to reject manuscripts; (4) disclose source of idea and funding for supplement and related products; (5) advertising in supplements should follow primary journal policies; (6) readers must be enabled to distinguish supplement pages from ordinary editorial pages; (7) editors must not accept personal favors or direct remuneration from supplement sponsors; (8) secondary publication in supplements should be identified by citation of the original paper; (9) same principles of authorship and disclosure apply to supplements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These principles preserve editorial independence and transparency when external funding or guest editors are involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic publishing, linking, preservation, and archiving
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles of print and electronic publishing are identical, but electronic publishing raises versioning, link stability, and preservation issues. Journals should be cautious about external linking and state they do not endorse content on linked sites; permanent preservation of articles on the journal website or in independent archives is essential; removing an article entirely is almost never justified; deposition in multiple archives is encouraged; if removal is necessary for legal reasons, provide a detailed reason and retain article in internal archive; nonarticle web pages should show last updated dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure link policies are explicit (no endorsement), archive content for historical record, and plan for transfer of journal files to a responsible third party in case of termination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising policy and editorial control over ads
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should have formal, explicit, written advertising policies for print and electronic versions. Advertising must not dominate journals or influence editorial decisions; advertisements should be clearly identifiable and editors should have final authority to approve and enforce advertising policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice prohibits selling advertisements intended to be juxtaposed with editorial content. Journals should not carry advertisements for products proven to be seriously harmful to health. Editors should ensure enforcement of regulatory or industry standards and consider publication of criticisms of advertisements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interactions with media and embargo practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals’ interactions with media should balance public interest and accurate reporting with need for vetted, peer-reviewed information. An embargo system may be used to prevent premature media reporting and to create a level playing field for reporters; editors can arrange agreements with authors not to publicize while under consideration and with media not to release stories before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embargo systems operate on the honor system; widespread noncompliance would dissolve them. Editors should weigh benefits of embargos (accurate reporting, orderly transmission, economic stability) against criticisms (impeding rapid dissemination).
